Lessons.Title: The Areas of Squares and Their Side Lengths
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: connect area of a square with the square of its side length, and determine an unknown side by using a nonnegative square root.

Construct paper square tiles with side lengths 1,2,3,4 and compare the number of unit-square tiles. The relationship A=s² means a square with area 25 has side length 5 units, not ±5, because physical lengths are nonnegative.
Original student task: use an accessible grid to draw squares with areas 4,9,16 and label sides; explain why 5 square units does not give a whole-number side. A teacher assesses the drawings.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area of square
KeyConcepts.Definition: Surface measurement of a square of side s.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square root of area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Nonnegative length whose square equals area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Non-square area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive area may require irrational side length.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area from side
WorkedExamples.Question: Square side length 4. What area?
WorkedExamples.Check: Four rows of four unit squares.

WorkedExamples.Title: Side from area
WorkedExamples.Question: Square area 25. What is its side?

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate side
WorkedExamples.Question: Square area 5. Is its side between 2 and 3?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding two sides to calculate area.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Square area multiplies length by width.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting negative physical side.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Distinguish algebraic x²=A from length s=√A.

SummaryPoints: Side length is the principal square root.
Not all square areas have integer side lengths.

Visuals.Title: Side length versus square area
Visuals.Description: A square of edge s has area s².

Lessons.Title: Side Lengths and Areas
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: reason about changes in square area when the side is scaled and infer the relationship between area factors and side factors.
Doubling the side length creates four times as much area, because both length and width double. If the area grows by factor 9, the side length grows by factor 3.
Compare original squares of side 2 and side 6; draw an array showing nine copies of the smaller square fitting the larger. A teacher judges the visual reasoning and correspondence.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Ratio of new square area to old square area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Side factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Positive square root of an area ratio.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Lengths and areas use different units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: side in cm, area in cm².
KeyConcepts.Example: Square side 6 cm has area 36 cm².

WorkedExamples.Title: Double side
WorkedExamples.Question: Square side 2 becomes side 4. Compare areas.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recover side factor
WorkedExamples.Question: Area increases from 9 to 144. By what factor did side grow?
WorkedExamples.Method: Take square root of area ratio.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming area scales linearly with side.
Using square-area units for side length.

SummaryPoints: Side scaling k changes square area by k².
Area factor reveals side factor through square root.

Visuals.Title: Doubling length quadruples square area
Visuals.Description: From edge 2 to 4, area rises from 4 to 16, factor four.

Lessons.Title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: distinguish rational numbers, which equal ratios of integers with nonzero denominator, from irrational numbers whose decimal expansions do not terminate or repeat.

Square roots of nonsquare positive integers such as √2 are irrational. A decimal like 0.333… is rational because it repeats and equals 1/3. A measured decimal approximation does not make an exact irrational number rational.
Construct a number-card sort using 1/2, √4, √2, 0.125, 0.333… and π. A teacher checks explanations and exact classifications rather than approximated display strings.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rational number
KeyConcepts.Definition: Can be written a/b with integers a,b and b≠0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Irrational number
KeyConcepts.Definition: Real number with no exact integer ratio.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Its decimal does not terminate or eventually repeat.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact versus approximation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rounded decimal is not equality of real values.
KeyConcepts.Example: Irrational cannot be fully represented by finite decimals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify √2
WorkedExamples.Question: Is √2 rational?
Steps: The positive square root √2 has no exact integer ratio.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify repeating decimal
WorkedExamples.Question: Is 0.333… rational?
WorkedExamples.Check: Repeat pattern determines an exact fraction.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming an irrational rounded to 1.41 becomes rational exactly.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An approximation is not the exact value.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling every infinite decimal irrational.

SummaryPoints: Irrational decimals never terminate or repeat.
Use exact notation and approximation honestly.

Lessons.Title: Square Roots on the Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: construct and locate square roots such as √2 on a number line, using geometric lengths and squared-distance reasoning.
A right triangle with legs 1 and 1 has hypotenuse √2 by the Pythagorean relation. Transfer its length with compass or paper strip from zero to mark √2 on a positive number line.
Sketch and annotate the construction rather than only writing 1.414. Teacher evaluation is necessary for a valid geometric placement and scale.

KeyConcepts.Title: Geometric square root
KeyConcepts.Definition: An irrational length may be constructed from right triangles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Number-line transfer
KeyConcepts.Definition: Mark a constructed length starting from 0.

KeyConcepts.Title: Approximate position
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare squares of adjacent decimals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unit triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Find diagonal of a unit square.

WorkedExamples.Title: Bound √2
WorkedExamples.Question: Show 1.4<√2<1.5.
Steps: Positive square root is between them.

WorkedExamples.Title: Locate √9
WorkedExamples.Question: Where is √9 on number line?
Steps: √9=3, so mark the third positive unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Plotting √2 at the integer 2.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The square root is smaller than its radicand in this range.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using 1.4 as exact √2.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use exact √2 and mark approximate location.

SummaryPoints: Irrational square roots represent real lengths.
Keep exact and approximate values separate.

Lessons.Title: Reasoning About Square Roots
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: bound and approximate square roots by comparing perfect squares and using numerical reasoning with positive values.
To estimate √30, start from 25<30<36, so 5<√30<6, then refine using decimals. For nonnegative square roots, squaring preserves order, allowing useful checks.
Make an original table of nearby squares to locate √30 and √50. A teacher reviews estimation and why a proposed bound is mathematically valid.

KeyConcepts.Title: Bounding squares
KeyConcepts.Definition: Bracket a radicand between known perfect squares.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decimal refinement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare squared tenths or hundredths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Principal root
KeyConcepts.Definition: Positive or zero square root of a nonnegative radicand.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Averaging bounding roots and calling it exact.
Squaring negative bounds without checking order.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Squaring is not order-preserving across negatives.

Lessons.Title: Finding Side Lengths of Triangles
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use right-triangle geometry to relate two perpendicular sides and the hypotenuse, and identify which sides are legs.

The Pythagorean theorem applies only to right triangles. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and must be the longest side. A drawn slanted side is not automatically the hypotenuse unless the right angle is identified.
Draw a 3-by-4 rectangle corner and connect endpoints to construct the right-triangle diagonal. Teacher review checks perpendicularity and correct side labels.

Independently authored Edulytiks instructional content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/8/6/preparation.html . Publisher figures and assessments are not duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Legs
KeyConcepts.Definition: The two sides that form the right angle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Hypotenuse
KeyConcepts.Definition: Side opposite the right angle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Right-angle condition
KeyConcepts.Definition: Angle between legs must equal 90°.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not use theorem for arbitrary triangle.
KeyConcepts.Example: A triangle with sides 3,4,6 is not right.

WorkedExamples.Title: Identify wrong longest side
WorkedExamples.Question: Can 3 and 4 be legs with c=6 in a right triangle?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using any triangle as right.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Locate and verify the right angle.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Labeling shorter side as hypotenuse.

SummaryPoints: Hypotenuse² equals sum of leg squares.

Visuals.Title: Exact right triangle triples
Visuals.Description: Original right-triangle numeric verification of a²+b²=c². It supplements but does not replace a labeled proof diagram.

Lessons.Title: A Proof of the Pythagorean Theorem
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: develop an area-based proof of a²+b²=c² using four congruent right triangles in a larger square, not merely plug numbers into the formula.

Arrange four congruent right triangles of legs a,b and hypotenuse c inside a square of side a+b. One arrangement leaves a central square of side c; its area is (a+b)²−4(ab/2). Expanding gives a²+b²=c².

Create a first-party paper-piece rearrangement with four labeled triangles, explain why the center is a square, and account for all pieces. Teacher review of construction and proof is required; a numeric exercise alone does not certify proof understanding.

KeyConcepts.Title: Large square area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area of enclosing square of side a+b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Four right triangles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each triangle has area ab/2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Central square
KeyConcepts.Definition: The remaining shape has side c, the hypotenuse.

WorkedExamples.Title: Derive formula
WorkedExamples.Question: Subtract four triangles from square (a+b)².
WorkedExamples.Check: Both descriptions cover the same enclosed area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check 3-4 proof
WorkedExamples.Question: For legs 3 and 4, find c² by rearrangement.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using numerical examples as a complete universal proof.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A few triangles do not establish all right triangles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting the four triangles in area count.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Then the central region is miscomputed.

SummaryPoints: Rearrangement proves the theorem by equal area.
Four triangles and the central square fill one larger square.

Visuals.Title: Numerical decomposition for Pythagoras
Visuals.Description: For a=3, b=4: outer square side 7 has area 49, four triangles total area 24, inner c²=25. This is NOT the actual visual proof.

Lessons.Title: Finding Unknown Side Lengths
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve for an unknown leg or hypotenuse in a right triangle, recognizing when subtraction versus addition of squares is appropriate.
The largest side c is the hypotenuse; if c and leg a are known, the missing leg b=√(c²−a²). Check that c>a>0 so the radicand is positive in a nondegenerate triangle.
Model a ladder as a right-triangle hypotenuse and its wall distance as a leg. Teacher reviews realism of perpendicular assumptions and units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing hypotenuse
KeyConcepts.Definition: Both legs known.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing leg
KeyConcepts.Definition: Hypotenuse and one leg known.

KeyConcepts.Title: Feasible side lengths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Hypotenuse must exceed each nonzero leg.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find hypotenuse
WorkedExamples.Question: Right triangle legs 8 and 15. Find c.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject impossible input
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a right triangle have hypotenuse 5 and leg 6?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding squares when finding a missing leg.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That would make the leg longer than hypotenuse.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using negative length.

Visuals.Title: Determine unknown hypotenuses
Visuals.Description: Original right-triangle numeric verification of a²+b²=c². It supplements but does not replace a labeled proof diagram.

Lessons.Title: The Converse
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use the converse of the Pythagorean theorem to test whether a triangle is right, and distinguish a proof from a simple diagram appearance.
For side lengths a≤b≤c, equality a²+b²=c² establishes a right triangle; if not equal, the triangle is not right. The triangle must satisfy ordinary triangle inequalities as well.
Sort independently prepared side triples into right and non-right groups with exact squared sums. Teacher checks the logical converse and classification.

Independently authored Edulytiks instructional content informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8 (2017–2019), CC BY 4.0. Exact source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/8/9/preparation.html . Publisher figures and assessments are not duplicated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pythagorean converse
KeyConcepts.Definition: If a²+b²=c² for a valid triangle with c longest, it is right.

KeyConcepts.Title: Longest-side choice
KeyConcepts.Definition: c is largest length before applying converse.

KeyConcepts.Title: Triangle validity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Any two side lengths sum greater than third.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject invalid triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Can sides 2,3,6 form a triangle?
Steps: The segments cannot close into a triangle.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using any side as c.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Converse requires longest side for c.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Testing Pythagoras before confirming triangle exists.

SummaryPoints: Ensure a valid triangle and longest side.

Lessons.Title: Applications of the Pythagorean Theorem
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: apply right-triangle distances in real contexts while identifying perpendicular sides, choosing units and interpreting a calculated length.

A 6-meter eastward and 8-meter northward displacement makes a right angle, giving straight-line displacement √(6²+8²)=10 m. Distinguish straight distance from travel along the two orthogonal paths (14 m).
Draw an original map with scale, perpendicular axes and a destination. Explain when right-angle assumptions are justified. Teacher checks the diagram and real-world interpretation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perpendicular displacement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two movements at 90° form triangle legs.

KeyConcepts.Title: Path length
KeyConcepts.Definition: Total length along segments.

KeyConcepts.Title: Direct distance
KeyConcepts.Definition: Hypotenuse between start and end.

WorkedExamples.Title: Street-grid distance
WorkedExamples.Question: Walk 6 m east, then 8 m north. Find direct distance.

WorkedExamples.Title: Ladder context
WorkedExamples.Question: Ladder 5 m long reaches wall at 4 m. Ground foot distance?

WorkedExamples.Title: Diagonal rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: Room 9 m by 12 m. Floor diagonal?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding leg lengths for straight distance.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That gives path travel, not direct hypotenuse.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the theorem on nonperpendicular measurements.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The condition must be a right angle.

SummaryPoints: Keep traveled and direct distances distinct.

Visuals.Title: Shortest path after perpendicular travel
Visuals.Description: Original right-triangle numeric verification of a²+b²=c². It supplements but does not replace a labeled proof diagram.

Lessons.Title: Finding Distances in the Coordinate Plane
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: derive and use the coordinate distance formula from horizontal and vertical displacements and Pythagorean theorem.
Two points (x₁,y₁),(x₂,y₂) determine horizontal difference Δx and vertical difference Δy. Euclidean distance is √(Δx²+Δy²), symmetric in point order and never negative.
Plot a pair of points with negative coordinates, draw its right-triangle legs, and explain why differences rather than raw coordinates enter the formula. Teacher checks the constructed visual.

KeyConcepts.Title: Horizontal change
KeyConcepts.Definition: Difference in x-coordinate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertical change
KeyConcepts.Definition: Difference in y-coordinate.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distance formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: Hypotenuse from coordinate differences.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute signed-point distance
WorkedExamples.Question: Distance between (−2,1) and (4,9)?
WorkedExamples.Check: Sign of start x is handled correctly.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding raw coordinates instead of differences.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Translation of both points should not change distance.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting negative distance.

SummaryPoints: Distance is invariant under common translations.

Visuals.Title: Distance by coordinate differences
Visuals.Description: From (−2,1) to (4,9), Δx=6 and Δy=8, so distance is 10. A coordinate grid is separately required.

Lessons.Title: Edge Lengths and Volumes
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: connect the volume of a cube with its edge length and estimate how volume changes under uniform 3D scaling.
A cube with edge e has V=e³. Doubling edge produces eightfold volume. Given volume 125 cubic units, the positive cube root gives edge 5 units.
Build 2×2×2 and 3×3×3 cube arrays from unit cubes or sketches, and explain why their volumes are 8 and 27. Teacher review of counting layers is required.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cube volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: All three edge dimensions are e.

KeyConcepts.Title: Uniform scale volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: Scale each edge by k.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse edge
KeyConcepts.Definition: Positive cube root of volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Double cube edge
WorkedExamples.Question: A cube edge grows from 2 to 4. Volume factor?

WorkedExamples.Title: Inverse volume
WorkedExamples.Question: Cube volume 125 cubic units. Find edge.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Squaring edge for cube volume.
Applying square root instead of cube root to volume.

SummaryPoints: Cube volume scales with third power.

Visuals.Title: Cubic volume changes with edge length
Visuals.Description: A cube with side length s has three equal dimensions and exact volume s³ cubic units.

Lessons.Title: Cube Roots
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret cube roots as inverse operations of cubing, including negative radicands and perfect cubes, and compare them with square roots.
The real cube root of −8 is −2 because (−2)³=−8. Unlike real square roots of negative numbers, real cube roots exist for every real input. Use exact notation ∛n and check by cubing.
Sort powers and inverse roots with original cards, including −27, 0, 1, 64 and 125. A teacher checks inverse-operation explanations.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cube root
KeyConcepts.Definition: Unique real x with x³=a.

KeyConcepts.Title: Negative cube root
KeyConcepts.Definition: Odd power keeps sign.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cube-square distinction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Square root of negative number is not real, but cube root is.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Odd exponent is invertible over reals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare 0 root
WorkedExamples.Question: What is ∛0?
Steps: No nonzero real x has x³=0.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring sign of negative radicand.
Giving ± for a cube root.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cubic is one-to-one over real numbers.

SummaryPoints: Negative numbers have negative real cube roots.

Visuals.Title: Real cube roots preserve negative signs
Visuals.Description: Each cube root r satisfies r³=x even for negative x.

Lessons.Title: Decimal Representations of Rational Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: connect fractions to terminating and repeating decimal expansions using division, and explain why a repeating decimal can still represent an exact rational value.
Long division for 1/4 terminates at 0.25, while 1/3 repeats 0.333…. Any rational fraction in lowest terms with denominator factors only 2 and 5 has a terminating base-ten decimal.
Use original long-division diagrams and compare 3/8, 2/3 and 1/7. The teacher checks reasoning about remainders and repetition.

KeyConcepts.Title: Terminating decimal
KeyConcepts.Definition: Finite decimal digits after which representation ends.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equivalent to denominator with prime factors 2 and/or 5 in lowest terms.

KeyConcepts.Title: Repeating decimal
KeyConcepts.Definition: An eventual digit cycle extending indefinitely.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact rational
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction defines exact value regardless of decimal length.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert 3/8
WorkedExamples.Question: Write 3/8 as decimal.
Steps: Long division yields further digits 7 and 5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert 2/3
WorkedExamples.Question: Write 2/3 as decimal.
Steps: The same remainder produces digit 6 repeatedly.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling repeating decimal irrational.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use long division or geometric series.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating truncated 0.66 as exact 2/3.

SummaryPoints: Rational decimals terminate or eventually repeat.

Lessons.Title: Infinite Decimal Expansions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: distinguish infinite repeating decimal expansions from nonrepeating ones and reason about exact values and rationality.

An infinite decimal such as 0.121212… repeats and is rational. A nonterminating nonrepeating expansion can represent an irrational number; however, a finite prefix never proves the continuation pattern.
Write an original repeating pattern, derive 0.121212…=12/99=4/33, and compare with irrational √2. A teacher reviews explanations about the role of the infinite tail.

KeyConcepts.Title: Infinite repeating
KeyConcepts.Definition: Digit block repeats forever.

KeyConcepts.Title: Infinite nonrepeating
KeyConcepts.Definition: No eventual periodic digit block.

KeyConcepts.Title: Finite prefix limit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Known digits alone do not prove full infinite pattern.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distinguish finite observation and defined infinite rule.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1.4142 could prefix infinitely many different numbers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inferring irrationality solely from infinite digits.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An infinite repeating decimal is rational.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating decimal approximation as exact root.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Finite truncations have small but nonzero error.

Lessons.Title: When Is the Same Size Not the Same Size?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare display areas when screen aspect ratios differ, distinguishing equal diagonal lengths from equal surface areas.

A rectangular screen with width w and height h has area A=wh, diagonal d=√(w²+h²). For fixed diagonal d and aspect ratio w:h=a:b, the dimensions are w=da/√(a²+b²), h=db/√(a²+b²). Different ratios can give different areas despite the same diagonal.

Compare a 3:4 screen and a 9:16 screen of equal diagonal 20 units. Compute both exact areas and explain why diagonal alone is insufficient. A teacher checks a properly labeled drawing and comparison assumptions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Aspect ratio
KeyConcepts.Definition: Width-to-height ratio of a rectangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Diagonal relation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pythagorean relation for rectangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area at fixed diagonal
KeyConcepts.Definition: For ratio a:b and diagonal d, A=d²ab/(a²+b²).
KeyConcepts.Rule: Area depends on ratio, not only diagonal.

WorkedExamples.Title: 3:4 screen area
WorkedExamples.Question: Screen ratio w:h=3:4 and diagonal 20. Find area.
Steps: To reach diagonal 20 multiply both dimensions by 4.

WorkedExamples.Title: 9:16 screen area
WorkedExamples.Question: Ratio 9:16 and diagonal 20. Express exact area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Width and height individually satisfy the 20-unit diagonal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare equal diagonals
WorkedExamples.Question: Which has larger area for equal diagonal 20, ratios 3:4 or 9:16?
Steps: The 3:4 screen has larger area despite equal diagonal.
WorkedExamples.Check: Diagonal alone does not determine screen area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using diagonal as if it were the rectangle height.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Diagonal is hypotenuse, not an edge.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Derive dimensions from ratio and Pythagoras.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claiming equal diagonal means equal area.

SummaryPoints: Screen diagonal does not uniquely determine area.
Aspect ratio constrains width and height.
Use exact geometry with specified dimensions.
